mcqs.question: In the classic prev/curr/next reversal walk, why must `next` be saved before `curr.next` is reassigned?
options: It isn't necessary — the order doesn't affect correctness
Saving it makes the algorithm run in O(log n) instead of O(n)
Doubly linked lists require it but singly linked lists don't
Once `curr.next` is overwritten, the original forward link is gone, so the walk would lose the rest of the list
mcqs.explanation: Reassigning `curr.next` destroys the only reference to the rest of the unreversed list; if you haven't saved that pointer first, you can no longer advance forward and the remaining nodes become unreachable. This is a correctness issue that applies equally to singly and doubly linked lists, not a performance detail.

mcqs.question: In the recursive reversal `reverse_list(head)`, what does the value returned by the base case represent?
options: The new head of the entire reversed list, passed unchanged through every returning call
The node immediately before `head`
A freshly reversed copy of just the current node
The length of the list
mcqs.explanation: The base case fires on the original list's last node, and that node becomes the new head — every enclosing call simply forwards that same value back up without modifying it, only rewiring `next`/`head.next` pointers around it. It isn't a predecessor reference, a partial copy, or a count.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks you to reverse a list "without using extra space." Why does the recursive solution fail that constraint even though it allocates no array or hash map?
options: It doesn't fail — recursion never uses extra memory
It requires the list to be doubly linked
It uses O(n) call-stack frames, one per node, which is extra space even without an explicit data structure
It has worse time complexity than the iterative version
mcqs.explanation: Each recursive call adds a stack frame that persists until the base case returns, so a list of n nodes uses O(n) stack space — space that's easy to overlook because there's no visible container. Both versions have the same O(n) time, and recursion works fine on singly linked lists.

mcqs.question: In k-group reversal, why does the algorithm first walk k steps to check nodes exist before reversing anything?
options: To compute the total list length
To confirm a full group of k nodes exists, since reversing a partial final group and having nothing correct to reconnect it to would corrupt the list
To find the exact middle of the list
Walking ahead is unnecessary — it's purely a style choice
mcqs.explanation: If fewer than k nodes remain, the problem calls for leaving that remainder unreversed — reversing it anyway with no valid reconnection target would scramble pointers. The check exists specifically to detect that case before committing to any pointer rewiring, not to measure the whole list's length or find its midpoint.

mcqs.question: After reversing one group of k nodes, which node needs its `next` pointer explicitly reconnected to the following segment?
options: The node that was originally first in the group, which is now the group's tail
The node that was originally last in the group, which is now the group's head
None — reversal automatically wires the join
Only the very last node of the entire list
mcqs.explanation: Reversal flips the group internally, turning its original first node into the new tail — and that node's `next` still holds a stale reference into the middle of its own just-reversed group unless you explicitly repoint it at the next segment. The original last node became the new head and needs no such fix; skipping this step silently corrupts the list rather than throwing an error.
